name: Skew deviation
aliases: skew deviation with ocular tilt reaction

clinicalPearls: An acquired vertical misalignment of the eyes caused by disturbance of the otolithic (utricular) vestibular pathways, not by a single ocular muscle palsy
It may occur alone or as part of the ocular tilt reaction with head tilt, ocular torsion and skew toward the lower eye
It is an important mimic of fourth nerve palsy and of other causes of vertical diplopia
The upright-supine test helps distinguish it: a skew deviation typically decreases when the patient lies supine
It usually signals brainstem or cerebellar disease, so acute skew with other signs may indicate stroke
Within the HINTS assessment of acute vestibular syndrome, skew deviation is a central (worrying) sign
reference.pathophysiology: Skew deviation results from an imbalance in the graviceptive otolithic pathways that project from the utricle through the brainstem to the ocular motor nuclei, producing a vertical divergence of the visual axes. Lesions of these pathways in the pons, medulla, midbrain or cerebellum disturb the normal tonic balance that keeps the eyes level, and when the full ocular tilt reaction occurs the head tilt, ocular torsion and hypotropia all deviate toward the side of a lower pontomedullary lesion (or opposite a higher one). Because these pathways lie in the posterior circulation, skew deviation frequently accompanies brainstem or cerebellar ischaemia.
additionalInvestigations: HINTS examination in acute vestibular syndrome
Upright-supine test to demonstrate reduction of the deviation when supine
MRI of the brain with attention to the brainstem and cerebellum
Orthoptic assessment including measurement of ocular torsion
Vascular risk-factor evaluation when stroke is suspected
redFlags: Acute onset with vertigo, ataxia or other brainstem signs
Any feature suggesting posterior circulation stroke
Reduced conscious level or rapidly evolving deficits
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the underlying cause; skew from a self-limiting or treatable lesion may resolve, but as a sign of brainstem or cerebellar stroke it carries the prognosis of that event.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing skew as a benign fourth nerve palsy and missing a stroke
Failing to perform HINTS in acute vestibular syndrome
Overlooking the associated ocular tilt reaction
Attributing vertical diplopia to orbital disease without considering a central cause
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Treat the underlying cause as the priority, activating an urgent stroke pathway when acute skew occurs with other central signs on HINTS assessment
Direct management of the causative posterior fossa lesion, whether ischaemia, demyelination, tumour or haemorrhage, with the relevant specialist team
Relieve vertical diplopia symptomatically with prisms or temporary monocular occlusion while awaiting resolution
Address vascular risk factors with antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy and blood pressure and lipid control when an ischaemic cause is confirmed
Arrange orthoptic follow-up to monitor the deviation and ocular torsion, reserving strabismus surgery for stable, persistent misalignment
Refer for multidisciplinary neurology and neuro-ophthalmology assessment
